translation:
Jivandasji Maharaj says: do not keep loving affection with Sakut people, nor keep their company; and have no dealings at all with a Salil devotee. But with those who practise exclusive (ananya) devotion, speak the thoughts of your heart openly, without hiding anything. Conduct yourself only according to the teaching received from your guru. Give up the company of Salil and Sakut, or else you will have to wander again through the four wombs of the eighty-four lakh species of life. I proclaim this loudly, beating the drum, so let the disciples of the true guru listen: Jivanji Maharaj has said that you must not associate with Sakut and Salil.

Salil people, along with their exclusive devotion, also worship Anadev (another deity, besides their chosen deity) — like a snake that keeps one hand in the milk and one in the curd, so that the curd spoils the milk as well; such is their conduct. True exclusive (ananya) devotees, however, are single-minded (ekanishtha) alone.

_manasyekam vachasyekam karmanyekam mahatmanam, manasyanyad vachasyanyat karye chanyad duratmanam_ (For noble souls, the mind, speech, and action are one and the same; for the base-minded, the mind thinks one thing, the speech says another, and the action does yet another.)

Noble, great souls behave the same way in mind, speech, and action, whereas base people think one thing in the mind, say something else with the mouth, and do yet another thing in action. Such people are counted as Salil.

_antar khole jarsu, kahe guruki vani, parsa patisu rusna, kahe ku kushalta_ (She opens her heart to an adulterous man, yet repeats the wise sayings of the guru's teaching — Parshuram asks: if she stays estranged from her own husband, how can any good come of it?)

Parshuram says: if a woman opens her heart freely before an adulterous man and behaves without restraint, yet also speaks the wise sayings of good saints, while remaining estranged from her own husband, then how can any true good come to her?

Salil and Sakut people have no single-mindedness, whereas single-mindedness exists among ananya devotees who are simple and guileless. Here is an illustration of this.

In a village of Vraj, an assembly of learned pandits was taking place. Everyone was describing their own exclusive devotion (ananyata), saying, "We do not accept any deity other than our chosen deity (Ishtadev)." (Some say they were describing the exclusive devotion of Shrimad Vallabhacharya Mahaprabhuji.) Just then a cowherd boy (gwalbal) arrived. He was told, "You people are ananya (exclusive), but I am fananya." Hearing this, the pandits fell into great confusion — everyone knows what "ananya" means, but what is "fananya"? Finally they all asked the boy for the meaning of "fananya." He said, "Listen — you people are ananya: you do not accept any deity other than your chosen deity, but you still know of the others. I, on the other hand, know of no one at all except my one and only Nanda's darling, dear Kanaiya (Krishna). As for believing or not believing in others — that is far too remote a matter for me even to consider." On hearing this boy's utterly truthful reply, the great brahmins bowed their heads before him and said, "Brother! You, who are fananya, are greater than us, who are merely ananya."

_to salilpe sakut bhalo, je kabahu pave par, salil duba kichme, jivan jal vina jaisi nav_ (So Sakut is better than Salil, for he may sometimes cross over to the far shore; Salil drowns in the mud — says Jivan — like a boat stranded without water.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that Sakut people are somewhat better than Salil people, because even though a Sakut worships Anadev, he may still (like Krishnadasji) sometimes get the chance to cross the ocean of worldly existence. Salil, however, worships many gods and also worships his chosen deity at the same time, and so, like a boat stuck fast in the mud for want of water, he ends up belonging nowhere. He falls from this side and from that, and wanders about ruined on every side.

In line 11, page 15, the revered Yadunath writes: "Salil — one who worships whatever deity he pleases, apart from the one appointed."

_salil bhagatku jivna, mat koi patiyay, kabahu sant sangat kare, kabahu sakutan mali jay_ ||7|| (Do not trust a Salil devotee at all, says Jivan — sometimes he keeps company with saints, and sometimes he goes and mixes with Sakuts.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: place no trust at all in a Salil devotee. At times he keeps the company of saints, and at other times he goes and mixes with the Sakuts.

A kavit by Chaturbhujdas, a cry of anguished appeal (gohai pokar):

_karm rat hari arpe, jani man anandvani jajai, karm krishnake ke to, kavan avkashaju bhajai, jyon sukh na lahat aru swad, nasikako udak pan kari, jadipi jathar-me jai, kahi gita ju avadhi pare, chaturbhuj moralidhar bhakti hit (var bajan), tanak salil nasht hi karat, jyon surasari jala kumbhme, suravrund kinchita parato_ (Chaturbhujdas says: only actions surrendered to Hari, done in devoted remembrance, are true; if one worships Anadev even while claiming great devotion to Krishna, calling that action "devotion to Krishna" makes no sense — like drinking water through the nose gives no taste or pleasure, and even if it reaches the stomach, it makes one retch and vomit before that. In the same way, if one worships Anadev while claiming devotion to Moralidhar, even a slight trace of Salil mixed in destroys the devotion entirely — just as a single drop of liquor dropped into a pot of sacred Ganga water spoils and defiles the whole pot.)

Chaturbhujdas says: one should act only after surrendering completely to God, becoming His refuge. Even though one knows that this alone is true devotion, if one still worships Anadev, then however much devotion to Krishna one may perform through one's actions, how can that worship truly count as devotion to Krishna? It is like drinking water through the nose — one gets no pleasure of taste at all, and even if the water does reach the stomach, a wave of nausea makes one retch and vomit before it gets there. In the same way, if one who is supposed to be a worshipper of Krishna-bhakti (devotion to Krishna) also worships Anadev, his state becomes just like that of a person drinking water through the nose. Chaturbhujdas says that if, without keeping one's aim fixed on devotion to Lord Moralidhar (Krishna), even the slightest trace of Salil-ness enters one's devotion, it destroys the whole of one's Krishna-bhakti — just as a single drop of liquor falling into a jar of Ganga water spoils and defiles the entire jar.

_pativratako dharm kahat ganika kahe kyon aavai, jor kahe to sharm(avar) karm kul nasht kahavai, jan ananya nij vrat karat (grahma) kaise salil sare, sakal dharm aru kul karm visare sevai jo ek hari, chaturbhuj kanchan aru kach jyon pheri shiar mrigraj jyo sam sare, kesar geru jyon ganiyo aru bhakt salil anin tyon_ (How can a courtesan ever be told the duty of a chaste wife — how could that duty ever come to her? If one insists on it, it is shameful, and it will only be called the ruin of one's family. In the same way, how can the practice of Salil-ness ever be reconciled with a devotee who upholds his vow of exclusive devotion? An exclusive devotee, holding fast to God alone, forgets and sets aside all other duties and family customs. Chaturbhujdas says there is as much difference between gold and glass, or between a jackal smeared in ochre calling itself the king of beasts, as between saffron and red ochre — that same difference exists between a true devotee and a Salil who calls himself an exclusive devotee.)

Chaturbhujdas says: even if a courtesan is taught the duty of a chaste wife, how could she ever actually become one? If she were called a wife, it would bring shame and would be said to destroy the honour of the family. In the same way, how could the practice of Salil-ness ever be accomplished by devotees who hold to the vow of exclusive, single-minded devotion? One who bears the vow of exclusive devotion and worships God alone forgets — sets aside — all other religious observances and family customs. Chaturbhujdas says there is as much difference between gold and glass as there is here. Just as it would be a sham for a jackal to smear itself with saffron-coloured ochre and call itself the lion, the king of beasts, so too it is when a Salil calls himself an exclusive (ananya) devotee.

Chaturbhuj has written the following kavit, laying stress on how one must give up the company of Salil.

_baru vichar man manjha, baru agni panjar kar, baru to byal avlamb, barut mrigraj ank (aalingan) bhare, baru barunalay kare pravesha, grasahi jala uksa, baru girivar chadhi shikhar, modpe (rudh) tahan deh adhah dhase, chaturbhuj moralidhar bhakt tav, bhul na sang salil kare, varu tan jo jay haribhajan jini haribhajan jat ravi tat dare_ (Better to enter a burning cage, or to be gripped in a serpent's coil, or to embrace the king of beasts, the lion — better to plunge into the ocean and be swallowed by its waters, or to climb the tallest peak of the Himalaya and hurl oneself down headfirst from its summit — than for a devotee of Lord Moralidhar to ever, even by mistake, keep the company of a Salil. Better that this body should perish while doing Hari-bhajan, says Chaturbhuj, than to give up Hari-bhajan; for even the sun, father of Yama, fears one who does Hari-bhajan.)

God Himself teaches and instructs His beloved devotee, so that the devotee understands that bad company disturbs one's devotion to God, and such company must be given up; one should not keep any companionship that creates an obstacle to remembering God. Whatever hardship it takes, one must bear it — even if bad company would bring some benefit, that benefit is worthless. Bad company must be given up. Whatever hardship must be borne, one should make every possible effort to escape it.

It is good for a devotee of Lord Moralidhar to resolve to act in just this way even towards his own worst enemy — with the thought: even if I must enter a burning cage, or be gripped in a serpent's coil, or come face to face with a lion, or plunge into the ocean, or climb to the summit of the tallest, highest peak of the Himalayas and be hurled down headfirst from there, I am ready to bear that suffering. But Chaturbhujdas says that even so, God's devotee will never, even by mistake, be ready to keep company with a Salil who would make him give up Hari-bhajan (devotional remembrance of Hari). Even if this body should perish while doing Hari-bhajan, that is better still. Even Surya, father of Yama, and Brahma, father of Surya, revere one who performs Hari-bhajan — so they can do nothing at all against a devotee of Hari.

Three kavits by Chaturbhujdas have been given here regarding giving up the company of Salil; let us also look at the kavit he wrote describing what a Salil is actually like.

_diksha mantra ju grahai, krishna kinkar ju kahavai, hari aaradhan karai, anadevan puni dhavai, karm dharm kul kaan, kaal kabahu na visarai, santan so ashraddha, kaam mati pasarai, aise salil sab nirakh ke, bhule na sang salil karai, haribhajan dar chaturbhuj na rahe, aru sahes maar jam jaal parai_ (Even one who has taken initiation and its mantra, and calls himself a servant of Krishna, who worships and adores Hari, yet still runs off to worship Anadev; who never forgets the ritual observances, customs, and family traditions handed down through the generations; who has no faith in the saints' teaching, and lets his mind run after selfish desire — having recognized such a Salil for what he is, do not, even by mistake, keep company with him. Chaturbhuj says: one who does not fear giving up Hari-bhajan will fall into Yama's snare and suffer his blows a thousandfold.)

Someone may have received initiation from a guru, taken the name of God and the name of Ram-Krishna, and let himself be called a devotee of Krishna, performing worship (aradhana) of Hari — and yet still worship Anadev as well; he clings to ritualistic works and observances, the customs and ways handed down through his family lineage across the four Vedic traditions, the customs of his caste and clan, and never forgets to celebrate the dark, worldly festivals and observances. Such a person, who places no faith in the teaching of the guru and the saints, and instead lets his mind run, sullied, after self-interested ritual — such a Salil, meaning one whose devotion lacks single-minded exclusivity — must never be kept company with, even by mistake, because his company will not let devotion to Hari remain steady within our hearts, and as a result we would fall into the noose of Yamaraj and have to endure his blows.

In the Samagam it is strongly urged that we give up both the food and the company of a Salil. There is a Sanskrit shloka on this subject as well.

_avaishnavasya hastannam divya deshadupagatam, harei prasadam tirtha cha prayatnena vivarjayet_ (Food that comes from the hand of a non-Vaishnav, even if it has come from a divine realm, or even if it be the prasad of Hari or the sacred water from His feet, should be deliberately and carefully avoided.)

Food that has come through the hand of a non-Vaishnav should be carefully avoided, even if it has come from a divine abode, or is God's own prasad or the sacred water that has bathed His feet (charanamrit). The devotees have placed great emphasis on staying far away from the Salil, who has turned away from God.

_samarme laryo jahi, girihate giryo jai, gaganme phiryo jai pavakko dahisho, kananme rahyo jai, vyalkar gahyo jai, virahahu sahyo jai, aur kahya kahisho, halahal liyo jai, sarbas diyo jai, karvat liyo jai, varindhiko bahisho, aur duhkh yahute ju dusah kathin aiso jaiso kahun vimukh sang ekchhin rahisho_ (I could go and fight in battle, I could fall from a mountain, I could go whirling through the sky and be burnt by fire, I could go and live in the forest, I could let myself be seized by a serpent, I could bear separation — and what more shall I say — I could go and drink deadly poison, I could give away all I possess, I could be sawn in two, I could go and drown in the ocean, and I could bear any other suffering more unbearable and harder than these — but I could never bear to stay even for a single moment in the company of one who has turned away from God.)

If I must fight in war, I can fight; if I must fall from a mountain, that too is fine; if I must be whirled about in the sky, that too is fine; if I must be burnt in fire, that too is fine; I can live in the jungle, and even if a tiger devours me, that is fine; I can bear separation, and what more can I say — I could even drink deadly poison, I could be cut apart with a saw, I could drown in the sea — I am ready to bear even greater and more unbearable sufferings than these, but I could not stay even for a single moment in the company of one who has turned away from God.

In the Samagam, seventeen sakhis (couplets) are given to warn us against the Sakut.

_vyas sindh bhuja bhar bhetiye, sahiye tanki haan, salil bhagat nav bhetiye, vyase taji pahejaan_ ||1|| (Vyas says: I would rather embrace a lion with my arms and bear the injury to my body, but I would never meet with a Salil devotee — Vyas has given up all acquaintance with him.)

Vyasdas says: I would embrace a lion and bear whatever injury comes to my body, but I would not keep company with a Salil devotee, nor keep any acquaintance with him, nor have any dealings with him. Vyas, the exclusive devotee, has given him up entirely.

Trikamdas Gordhan has written a kundli (a chained-verse form) on this — see Diary (Samvat) 2025, page 74, on the kundli.

_vyasa vadhkun bhetiyo, sahiyo tanki haan, salil bhagat na bhetiyo, chhod dije pahijaan, chhod dije pahichaan, sangathi sukrit jave, adke vadhe abhadaat, paarkun paatak laave, samjo sadguru saan, garghav sam nav letiyo, sahiyo tanki haan, vyas vadhku bhetiyo_ (Vyas would meet even a tiger and bear the harm done to his body, but he would never meet a Salil devotee — give up all acquaintance with him. Give up acquaintance with him, for his company destroys good deeds; contact with him increases defilement and brings another's sin upon us. Understand the wisdom given by the true guru, and do not roll about like a donkey in that filth. Bear the harm to the body — Vyas would meet a tiger rather than meet a Salil.)

Vyasji says: it is acceptable to embrace and meet a tiger, and to bear whatever injury the body suffers because of it, but do not mix with a Salil devotee, and give up all acquaintance and dealings with him. Give up all relations with a Salil, for his company will destroy our merit and good deeds. Keeping contact with him will increase our defilement and untouchability and will bring another's sin upon us. Understand well the wisdom that the true guru has given. Do not roll about in the dust of Salil-ness like a donkey — that is, do not, like a fool, form any inward bond with a Salil. Vyasdasji says: if embracing a tiger injures the body, bear it — but do not, under any circumstance, keep company with a Salil.

_vyasa vadhkun bhetiye, sahiye tanki haan, salil bhagat no bhetiyo, chhod dije pahichaan, chhod dije pahichaan, sangate sukrit naase, chhodvi satsang gang, halahal vikhadan pase, salil sakutna chhanyade, bhulechukena besiye, sahiye tanki haan, vyas vadhku bhetiye_ (Vyas would meet a tiger and bear the harm to his body, but never meet a Salil devotee — give up acquaintance with him. Give up acquaintance with him, for his company destroys our good deeds and makes us abandon the Ganga of holy company (satsang, the fellowship of the devout), bringing us near the deadly poison of worldly desire instead. Never sit, even by mistake, in the shade of a Salil or a Sakut. Bear the harm to the body — Vyas would meet a tiger rather than meet a Salil.)

Vyasji says: it is good to embrace a tiger rather than to meet with, or keep acquaintance and dealings with, a Salil devotee, for his company destroys our merit and good deeds. His company makes us give up the Ganga of satsang and instead pours into us the deadly, powerful poison of maya — sensual desire and the like. So, even by mistake, one should never go into the shade or the ashram of a Salil or a Sakut. Vyasdasji says: it is good to embrace a tiger and bear the harm it does the body, but one must never make contact with a Salil.

The same essential meaning is stated also in the Sankhyayana Samhita.

_aalapaan daata samsparshaat nivasaat sah bhojanaat, santa charatiha paapaani taula bindu khimbhaasi. aalinganam varam manyo vyaal vyaghra jalaukasaam, na sangam shalya yuktaanaam naana devakai sevinaam_ (Better to embrace a snake, a tiger, or a leech than to keep company with those whose devotion is mixed with the thorn of worshipping various gods; for through conversation, direct contact, dwelling together, and eating together with such people, sin spreads within us, drop by drop, like a drop of oil spreading across water.)

It would be better to embrace a tiger, or even a whole group of tigers, and be caught in their claws, than to keep company with worshippers of the various Anadevs, whose company wounds us like a spear — because through conversing with them, through unguarded contact, through living with them, or through eating with them, sins spread within us just as a drop of oil spreads through water.

There is also a saying of Harivamshji on this.

_khanpan tahan kijiyo, rasik mandali manhi, jinke aur upasna, tako lijiye naahi_ (Take food and drink only within the company of fellow devotees who share your own loving devotion; never accept the food of those whose worship is directed elsewhere.)

Harivamshji says that we should eat and drink only in the company of those who share the same taste and language of devotion as we do; we should never accept food from those whose worship is different from our own — such food is not truly fit to be accepted.

_bhagati hai bahu bhaantki, jinke bohotek bhed, bina vivek milvo, tahan man pave ati khed_ (Devotion is of many kinds, with many different varieties within it; to associate with others without discernment brings the mind great sorrow in the end.)

Das Kabirji says: devotion to God is of many kinds, with different types — such as with desire, without desire, love-marked devotion, the mood of a servant, of a friend, of parental love, of the beloved, of sweetness, of enmity, of pure loving devotion, and so on. So, if one mixes with others without understanding what is fitting and what is not, then later, when differences of opinion arise in the mind, one is filled with deep regret.

_vyas sakut geheri chhandiye, gunka kije naar, hari dasi jo hoyegi, to kul na aape gaal_ ||2|| (Vyas says: give up a Sakut wife entirely, and instead make a courtesan your wife — for if she becomes a maidservant of Hari, she will bring no disgrace upon the family.)

Vyasdasji says that if one's wife is a Sakut, she should be given up; and, if it comes to it, one should rather choose to accept a courtesan — a woman who marries by virtue, or one who marries by outward attraction — as wife, because if she becomes a servant-devotee of God's devotees, our family and lineage will not be shamed or disgraced.

_triya jo va hoy haridasi, dusht mile aru man mile. varam shunya shala na cha varo dushtavrishabho, varam veshya patni na punaravinita kulavadhuh, varam vaso'ranye na punaravivekaadhipapure, varam pranatyago na punaradhamaanaamupagamah_ (If a wife is a servant of Hari, that is best; even meeting a wicked person and being of one mind with him is discussed here — better an empty cowshed than one occupied by a vicious bull; better a courtesan as wife than an ill-mannered, undisciplined wife of good family; better to dwell in the forest than in the city of an unwise king; better to give up one's very life than to associate with the base and the wicked.)

It is better for a cowshed to stand empty than for it to house a vicious bull. It is better to keep a courtesan as one's wife at home than to have a well-born wife who lacks humility. It is better to have to live in the forest than to have to live in the city of an unwise, indiscreet king. It is better to give up one's very life than to keep company with base, low people.

Harirayji, in the fifth verse of the Shikshapatra, has said:

_pratikulye yatha tyagah prabhvasambandhi vastutah, dhaneshu nisprihah sevopayogitvena rakshanam_ ||5|| (Just as one gives up any object that stands opposed to one's Lord, so too — though remaining free of any craving for wealth — one should protect and keep wealth only insofar as it is of use for His service.)

Just as anything that is of no use in the service of Thakorji (the Lord) is given up, so too, if wife, children, and the like are of no use in the service of Shri Thakorji, they are fit to be given up as well. One should not crave wealth; wealth should be kept and protected only by understanding it as something useful for the service of Shri Thakorji.

_kabir unche kulki kamini, na bhaje sarangpan, kulahi lajavai aapno, sudhi saapin jaan_ (Kabir says: a woman of high birth who does not worship Sarangpani, that is, Krishna, disgraces her own family — know her to be no different from a straight-fanged serpent.)

Das Kabirji says: a high-born woman who lives behind the veil, and who out of shame does not perform bhajan (devotional worship) of God, should be understood to be someone who disgraces her own family — exactly like a female serpent.

_duniyake dhokhe muzha, chale jo kulki kaani, tab kul phiska lajsi, jab le dharya masaani_ (Deceived by the world, one lives bound by the shame and honour of family and clan; but when at last one is carried to the cremation ground, it is then that the family's honour will truly turn pale with shame.)

This describes the anxious concern people have for worldly custom and family tradition, living their lives in accordance with the customs of the clan; but when your death comes and you must suffer torment in the abode of Yama, then it will become clear — whose family, and whose honour, will really have cause for shame.

_tulsi bhakt swapach bhala, jinke mukhme ram, uncha kulkun kya karun, jise satsang nahi vishwas_ (Tulsi says: even an outcaste devotee is better, if the name of Ram is in his mouth — what use is high birth to me, if that person has no faith in satsang?)

_jaj janma taani karmaani tadayus taan manovachah, nrinaam yoneha vishvaatmaa sevyate haririshvarah_ ||9|| _kim janmabhis tribhir veha shauklasaavitrayaajnikaih, karmabhir vaa trayi-proktaih pumso'pi vibudhaayusha_ ||10|| (Only that birth, those deeds, that lifespan, and that thought and speech are truly successful, O Prachetas, through which people worship Hari, the Lord who is the very Self of the universe, in this human form — all else is vain. What is the use, even of three exalted births as one born of the seed, through the sacred thread, and through the performance of sacrificial rites, or of a lifespan lasting as long as that of the gods, if the worship and knowledge of the God who bestows one's own being are not attained?)

Narad says: O Prachetas, that birth, that action, that lifespan, and that mind and speech alone should be considered fruitful and successful which are spent in the service of the Lord God, the Self of the whole universe — all the rest should be understood as fruitless. If one does not attain the service and knowledge of the God who has given us our very being, then what fruit is there even in the three exalted kinds of high birth — born of seed, of the sacred thread, or of sacrificial rites? None at all.

_yu bane nahi jivna, avala savli mel(sare), purusha puje ramku, sakut naari dher_ ||4|| (Says Jivan: it can never work out this way — a mismatched pairing cannot succeed — where the husband worships Ram, but the wife in his house is a Sakut.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that no good outcome can ever come from mismatched, roundabout arrangements. If a man worships Ram, but the woman in his house is a Sakut who worships Anadev, no true welfare can result.

_sharir sakutan parsate, gun gaanthko jai, raghupati risave jivna, to harijan kaise sahay_ ||5|| (If the body even touches a Sakut, the virtue we have gathered is lost; and if Raghupati (Ram) becomes displeased, says Jivan, how then can Hari's devotees come to our aid?)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: if our body even touches a Sakut, that is, if we keep any dealings with a Sakut, then whatever good quality of single-minded devotion we have gained will be lost, and God Himself will become displeased with us — so how, then, could the grace and help of the saints ever reach us?

_vyas sakut bhaiyaa, chhandiye aur kubere karan saman, taki paant na khaiye, nishche narak nikhaan_ ||6|| (Vyas says: even one's own brother, if he is a Sakut, must be given up, even if he equals Kuber or Karna in greatness; never eat in the same row with him, for it certainly leads to hell.)

Vyasdasji says: even if one's own brother rivals the greatness of Kuber or Karna, if he is a Sakut, all relations with him must still be given up. One should not even sit and eat with him in the same row (pankti). If we do eat with him, we will certainly fall into hell.

_vyas viveki bhagatsu, dradh kar kije prit, avivekiko sang tyaj, ehi bhagatki reet_ ||7|| (Vyas says: form a firm and unwavering love with the discerning devotee, and give up the company of the undiscerning — this is the true way of a devotee.)

Vyasdasji says: with a discerning, understanding devotee who truly grasps exclusive devotion, one should form a deep and firm love; but the company of an undiscerning person who does not truly understand should be given up — this is exactly the way that exclusive devotees have adopted for themselves.

_kabir sakut saga na bhetiye, apne kanth lagay, parmaarath bahe jai, paap rahe lapataay_ ||8|| (Kabir says: do not embrace even your own kinsman if he is a Sakut, clasping him to your own chest — the true purpose of your life will slip away, and sin will cling to you instead.)

Das Kabirji says that we must not keep close dealings with kinsmen and loved relatives who are Sakut. Keeping relations with them will destroy the essence of our single-minded devotion, and the sin of ill counsel and bad conduct will attach itself to us.

_sakut sakut sabko kahe jivna, kachhu sakutan sidhaan, ninda karveku shurma, nahi guru vachan pramaan_ ||9|| (Everyone says "Sakut, Sakut," says Jivan, yet few truly understand what marks a Sakut: he is a hero at slandering others, and does not accept the guru's word as authority.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: everyone keeps saying "Sakut, Sakut," but the chief mark of who a Sakut truly is, is this — such people are bold and fearless in slandering and reviling Vishnu-bhakti and Hari, guru, and saints, and they refuse to accept the authority of the guru's teaching.

_sakut sakut sabko kah, kachhu sakut subhav, harijanki ninda kare, anadevku dhaya_ (Everyone says "Sakut, Sakut," yet few know the true nature of a Sakut: he slanders the devotees of Hari, and runs after Anadev.)

The devotee says: everyone keeps saying "Sakut, Sakut," but what is the true, essential nature of a Sakut? It is this — he keeps slandering the saints, and he worships Anadev.

_kabir bhagat hazaari kapada, taame mal na samay, sakat kaali kaamli, bhaavai tahan bichhaay_ ||10|| (Kabir says: a devotee is like fine, costly cloth, in which no dirt can lodge; a Sakut is like a black woollen blanket, spread out wherever it pleases.)

Das Kabirji says: devotees and saints possess exalted virtues, like fine, costly, brilliant-white cloth, in which the dirt of bad company can find no lodging. Sakuts, however, are wicked in their deeds, like a black woollen blanket — and just as there is no harm in spreading such a blanket out anywhere at all, so too the Sakuts remain spread out everywhere, sunk in sensual pleasure and desire.

_yatha hi malinair vastrair yatra tatropavishyato, evam chalitachittastu chittaashesham na rakshati_ ||30|| (Just as a man wearing soiled clothes will sit down anywhere at all without discrimination, so too a man whose mind has once wavered no longer guards the rest of his conduct at all.)

Just as a man wearing soiled clothes will sit down anywhere at all, in dust or dirt, without a second thought, so too a man who has once fallen away from virtuous conduct no longer cares about maintaining any other good conduct — he becomes given over to every kind of misconduct.

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written sakhis about Salil and Sakut.

_sakut sang karva thaki, manushya ang abhaday, kabir sadguru kahi gaya, samajethi sukh thay_ ||1|| (Through keeping company with a Sakut, a person's very body becomes defiled — so said the true guru Kabir; understanding this brings true happiness.)

Trikamdas says that, through keeping company with a Sakut, our human birth falls into a condition as good as untouchable, weighed down with sin — so the true guru Kabir has said. So if we understand and follow this advice, our welfare will be secured.

_nachna kudna talku pitna, randiya khelki bhakti nahi_ (Dancing, jumping about, and beating out the rhythm — a widow's playful sport is not devotion.)

If we merely dance, leap about, and play the drums outwardly for show and call it devotion, such a feeble, pitiable, hollow display is not true devotion at all.

_salil sakutna sangathi, gun gaandhno jai, patit bani pachhaday jataan, vaaso narakmaan thai_ ||2|| (Through company with the Salil and the Sakut, the virtue we have gathered slips away; we become fallen and are thrown down, and end up dwelling in hell.)

Trikamdas says that through the company of the Salil and the Sakut, the good qualities within us are lost, and we become sinful; our condition becomes wretched, and in the end we must go to hell.

In verse 60, Mahadev has described the exclusive (ananya) Vaishnavs.

_jnana vairagya samyuktaah syur bhogino'pi param tapah, jivan-muktaash cha vijneyaa ananyaa vaishnavaah sada_ ||60|| (Those Vaishnavs who are joined with knowledge and dispassion perform the highest austerity even while enjoying worldly pleasures; the exclusive Vaishnavs are always to be known as liberated while yet living.)

Those Vaishnavs who possess knowledge and dispassion perform the highest austerity even while they enjoy worldly pleasures. Know that exclusive (ananya) Vaishnavs are always liberated while still living (jivanmukta).

Verse 60 describes the exclusive Vaishnav devotee. These Vaishnavs are liberated while living; they carry no burden of worldly entanglement connected with the body and such things. Outwardly they may appear to be enjoying luxurious pleasures, but inwardly they remain untouched by desire — their mind is fixed only on devotion to God. The word "ananya" breaks down as _na + anya_ — "that which is not other than oneself," that is, one who does not regard God as other than one's own self.

In Kalyan magazine, year 75, issue 6, it is written: _jis prakar shodhan kiya hua sankhiya anek prakarke rogonko mita deta hai, usi prakar dharmik bhavse bhoge hue bhog vasanase upar utha dete hain_ (Just as purified arsenic can cure many kinds of diseases, in the same way pleasures enjoyed in a spirit of religious devotion raise a person above desire, rather than binding them to it.)

In the life-story of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, there occurs the account of the hidden devotee Pundarik Vidyanidhi. His outer life was extremely luxurious. He would sleep on a costly couch, anointed with fragrant perfume, while servants waved fans over him and he used costly utensils — yet inwardly he was utterly free of craving. (Register 54, page 119.) An exclusive devotee has no attachment to the body and such things. It is said in the Gita:

_ananyaash chintayanto maam ye janaah paryupasate, teshaam nityaabhiyuktaanaam yogakshemam vahaamyaham_ ||22|| (Those who worship Me alone, thinking of nothing else, ever united with Me — for them, I Myself carry the burden of what they lack and what they already have.)

Those who, without worshipping any other deity, meditate on Me, the Supreme Self, and worship Me alone — for such people, who remain always single-minded and devoted to Me alone, I Myself carry, in every way and without even being asked, both their "yoga" (the attainment of what is beneficial but not yet possessed) and their "kshema" (the preservation of what is beneficial and already possessed).

Kabir has described what a true renunciant (tyagi) and ascetic (vairagi) is really like — he tells us what one endowed with knowledge and dispassion is like.

_apraapati chizka kya taje, praapti taje sohan tyaag hai, saraasi turang kau kya phaire, kathanath phaire soi vauji hai, jag bhavka gaavna kya gaave, anabhav gaave soi ragi hai, grahvanki vasna nash kare, kabir soi vairagi hai_ ||61|| (What is given up by giving up a thing never possessed? True renunciation is giving up what one has actually obtained. What is there in turning a horse that is already reined? True skill lies in turning back a wild, unbroken horse. What use is singing of the world's cycle of birth and rebirth — true song lies in singing of direct experience. He who destroys the very desire for home and forest alike — says Kabir — he alone is the true renunciate.)

Das Kabirji says: if you give up a thing you could never have had in the first place, what real renunciation is that? True renunciation is giving up what you have actually obtained. What great feat is it to turn a horse that already has a bridle and reins? Turning a truly wild, untamed horse — that is real horsemanship. What is the use of endlessly talking about the pleasures of this worldly ocean of birth and rebirth? He who sings, instead, the praises of that which lies beyond the ocean of birth and rebirth — he is the true lover of God. He who destroys the craving for both the household and the forest — he alone is the true renunciate.

_apraaptaku sab taje, praapti taje na koi, kahai kabir praapti taje, tyagi kahiye soi_ (Everyone gives up what they could never have gotten; no one gives up what they have actually obtained. Says Kabir: he who gives up what he has actually obtained — he alone should be called a true renunciate.)

Das Kabirji says: whatever we could never obtain in any case, everyone is quick to give up — but no one gives up what they have actually attained. So truly, only those who give up something they have actually obtained deserve to be called renunciates.

A sakhi of Kabirji is given here about saints and devotees whose minds are free of attachment, describing the strength of mind such devotees possess.

_gavan hi me rovna, rovan hi me rag, ek banaahi me ghar kare, ek dharahi me bairag_ ||1|| (Within singing itself lies weeping, and within weeping itself lies melody; one person makes his home even in the forest, while another lives in renunciation even within his own house.)

Das Kabirji says: what a strange spectacle this is — that one devotee, even while enjoying worldly pleasures within the household life, remains detached and free of attachment, and even in this state of detachment experiences the joy of loving devotion. On the other hand, those who have renounced the world and taken to life in the forest, even while living in the forest, indulge in pleasures and luxuries just like a householder. And the devotee who has taken up devotion right within his own household has begun to live, right there in the household, a life just like that of a true renunciate.

_vaneshu doshaah prabhavanti raginaam griheshu panchendriya nigrahastapah, akutsite karmani yah pravartate nivrittaraagasya griham tapovanam_ ||904|| (For one whose passions still cling, faults will arise even in the forest; controlling the five senses even while in the household is itself true austerity. For one who engages only in blameless action, and whose passions have truly ceased, the household itself becomes a forest of austerity.)

For a person who still has attachment to sensual objects, faults will arise even if such a person goes and lives in the forest. But for one who has cultivated restraint over his five senses even while living at home, that restraint itself is true austerity (tapa) in his mind. That is to say, for a person who remains occupied with good, blameless deeds and whose attachment to sensual objects has truly departed, the household itself becomes his forest of austerity.

One who disregards the householder life and goes to practise austerity in the forest — if such an ascetic later returns to the householder life, he is normally considered worthy of censure. Even though this is generally considered blameworthy, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu commanded Nityananda to give up his renunciate order (sannyas) and return to the householder life; yet he did not become an object of censure for it. Only hypocrites deserve censure.

_pahele dhar chhodya apna, pichhe paithe dhar maanhi, tulsi aise patitka, darshan kije naahi_ (First he gave up his own home; then afterwards he entered a home once more — Tulsi says: never even set eyes on such a fallen person.)

Tulsidas says: never even look upon a sinner who first, as an ascetic, gave up his householder's home, and then went back and entered the householder life once more.

_tulsi dharke dherme, dhadi dhadi tan chhin, kabahu ban banna phirai, kar karva kaupin, dharahi manhi ban kare, hari charane lauleen, tulsi aise santaaku, kaha karva kopin_ (Tulsi says: for such a false ascetic, moment by moment the body wastes away in worry over worldly household matters, though he wanders about with a water-pot and loincloth as if in the forest; but he who makes even his own home into a forest, absorbed lovingly at Hari's feet — for such a saint, says Tulsi, what need has he at all for a water-pot or a loincloth?)

Tulsidas says: there may be one whose body wastes away with worry in the whirl of the householder life, and who never actually wanders about from forest to forest holding a water-pot in hand, wearing a loincloth. Such a devotee, who lives out a forest-like life of devotion to God right within his own home — what need does such a saint have of a water-pot or a loincloth at all?

(In Raga Sarang.)

_kaha dar hai dharbaarko, jaake harde hariko samaran, dhokho naahi lagaarko. rahe dharmaanhe kaha ban maanhe, e to gyaan vichaarko, dhar chhodeki kaha bhalai, jutho khaaye sansaarko. tan vairagine man dharbaari, etu gyaan gamaarko, ek hi chhad anant hi laago, bhaar vahe sansaarko. hari chitaro harde dhaaro, gor gam gyaan apaarko, taaku karam kabhu nahi laage, sevak sarjanhaarko. sujha padhaavat gunka taari, vaaku vanaj vikaarko, ajaamel patit odhaariyo, naam liyo kartaako. seni dhana pipa aur napa, raanka jaat kumbharki, bhavna bhagatko khaando kaathkos pragat palat bhayo saarko. naanma kabira prem bhagat bhaye, aur rohidas chamaarku, dher betha govind grun gaave, bakhno sarjanharko_ (What fear of household bonds can there be for one whose heart holds the remembrance of Hari — no deceit of maya touches such a one at all. Whether one lives in the home or in the forest is merely a matter of thought and understanding; what good is there in leaving the home, if it only means living off the stale, cast-off food of the world? One whose body alone is renounced while the mind still runs after household matters — that is the foolish "wisdom" of an ignorant person; he leaves one home only to attach himself to countless others, and carries the burden of the world instead. Remember Hari, hold Him in your heart — this is the boundless wisdom the guru teaches; upon such a servant of the Creator, the bondage of karma never falls. He is taught the true worth of virtue; his trade is destroying vice. Ajamil, a fallen sinner, was delivered simply because he took the Name of the Creator. Seni, Dhana, Pipa, Napa, and Ranka of the potter caste were saved likewise; the devotee Bhavan's wooden sword was openly transformed into one of iron. Namdev, Kabir, and Rohidas the cobbler all became devotees of loving devotion — says Bakhno: seated right in one's own home, one may sing the praises of Govind, the Creator.)

Bakhnaji says: how could an exclusive devotee ever fear the illusion of household life, when the remembrance of Hari's Name is constantly running in his heart? Where that is so, no deceit of maya can remain at all. Whether one lives in a home or in a forest is a mere matter of imagination; what real benefit is there in leaving one's home, when the one who leaves must, in exchange, eat the leftover, tainted earnings of worldly people instead? Such people's bodies alone look like those of renunciates, while their minds remain exactly as worldly and household-bound as ever — this is the false understanding of such foolish people. They leave behind one single household and family, only to attach themselves to the company of countless worldly people instead, and take on the burdens and responsibilities of worldly life. Following the deep teaching of the guru, hold fast to God within your heart, as one worthy of your constant remembrance. A devotee of God, the Creator of the universe, is never bound by the fetters of karma. There was a courtesan whose trade was sensual indulgence, yet she taught her parrot to say the name of Ram, and God delivered her. Ajamil, who was a great sinner, took God's Name, and so God delivered him too. God rescued Seni Bhagat, Dhana Bhagat, Pipaji, and Napaji, as well as Ranka Bhagat, who was of the potter caste. For the devotee Bhagat Chavan, He turned a wooden sword into one of iron to help him. Namdev, Kabirji, and Rohidasji the cobbler became practitioners of loving devotion (prem-lakshana bhakti); staying seated right within their own homes, they practised devotion to God — and I, Bakhno, am likewise a devotee of the Creator of the universe, and a householder just the same.

(In Raga Desag.)

_sohi harijan grahi bhala, jaake harisu prit, raat divas visre nahi, aur harijan mit. kul karni sab bhetke, taje jug vahevaara, kshudha pramane udyam karai, aur taje pasaara. kanak kaamini kaalpana, parninda na jaane, bhaav bhagat hari pritsu, baana hi maane. kaam krodh mad matsar, abhimaan nivaarai, apna jiv sabhinka jaane, daya dharam vichaarai. kahat kabir kaljugme, harijan koi ek, aur sab swaangi sabai, jaake chit anek_ (That householder-devotee alone is blessed who has true love for Hari, never forgetting Him day or night, and who befriends only Hari's own devotees. Setting aside all family customs and worldly practices, he labours only enough to satisfy his hunger, and gives up all other display and excess. He harbours no thought of gold or women, and knows nothing of slandering others; his only mark and manner is loving devotion to Hari. He drives out lust, anger, pride, and envy; he regards his own soul as one with the souls of all beings, and reflects always on compassion and righteousness. Says Kabir: in this dark age of Kali, such a true devotee of Hari is one in a rare while — all the rest are mere pretenders, their minds scattered among countless things.)

_kabir sant samagam param sukh, aan alap sukh aur, maan sarovar hans hai, bagla thoro thaur. kabir sant sangat sabate saras, baana sat sab os, sant sabad parmaante, kaate kot adh dosh_ (Kabir says: fellowship with saints, satsang, is the highest happiness — all other happiness is little in comparison. As the swan lives on Man Sarovar lake, while the crane wanders here, there, and everywhere. Kabir says: the company of saints is sweeter than everything else; all worldly appearance is but a fleeting dewdrop. Through the authority of the saint's own word, crores of sins accumulated over past lives are cut away.)

Das Kabirji says: devotees who have true love for devotion to God within their hearts are excellent indeed, even if they are householders. They never, day or night, forget God and the company of Hari's devotees. They give up all worldly dealings bound up with family custom. They do not dwell on thoughts of gold or women, nor do they slander others. Their only fixed resolve is to practise devotion to God with loving feeling. They rid themselves of lust, anger, pride, envy, and arrogance. They understand their own soul as existing for the welfare of all beings, and they keep to the path of compassion and righteousness. Kabirji says that in this dark age of Kali, only a rare few such saints exist; all the rest are mere pretenders in disguise, whose hearts are filled with countless different desires.

Das Kabirji says: fellowship (samagam) with a saint is the highest happiness of all; every other happiness besides this is only slight, present in a very small measure. Just as the finest of souls, the swans, dwell in Man Sarovar lake, while hypocritical pretenders, like cranes, wander here and there...
